**(i) Cereals and legumes (5 marks)**

| Cereals | Legumes |
|---|---|
| Seeds of plants of the **grass family** (maize, rice, wheat, millet, sorghum, oats) | Seeds of plants of the **pea and bean family** (beans, cowpea, soya bean, peas, lentils, groundnut) |
| The seeds grow on **ears, cobs or panicles** | The seeds grow in **pods** |
| Rich in **carbohydrate (starch)**; low in fat | Rich in **protein** (soya bean and groundnut also in fat) |
| Contain a **lower amount of protein**, which is poor in lysine (a limiting amino acid) | The protein is richer in lysine but poor in methionine |
| The main **staple food** that gives bulk and energy; supplies B vitamins | A cheap **alternative to animal protein**, rich in iron, B vitamins and fibre; the plants fix nitrogen in the soil |

**(ii) Role of cereals in the diet (3 marks)**

1. They are the **main source of energy** (starch) and the staple food for most of the world.
2. They supply **B vitamins, iron and other minerals**, and **dietary fibre** (especially whole grains), which prevents constipation.
3. They supply **some protein**, which is complemented by legumes (for example maize with beans), and they are cheap and easy to store and prepare in many forms (flour, bread, pap, couscous, porridge).

**b.** (i) Define kilning and give its advantages in beer fermentation.

(5 marks)

(ii) With the aid of an equation briefly explain what happens during fermentation of corn beer.

(6 marks)

**(i) Kilning (5 marks)**

**Kilning** is the gentle **drying and heating of germinated (malted) grain in a kiln** to stop germination and reduce the moisture content, after the grain has been soaked and allowed to sprout.

Advantages in beer fermentation:

1. It **stops germination** at the stage when the amount of **amylase** (starch-splitting) enzymes is highest, and the enzymes are kept active if the temperature is not too high.
2. It lowers the moisture, so that the malt can be **stored without moulds or spoilage** and is easy to mill.
3. It develops the **colour, aroma and flavour** of the beer (dark malts at high temperature) and removes the raw, green taste.
4. It makes the malt brittle, so it is easy to crush, and it removes the rootlets and some unwanted substances.

**(ii) Fermentation of corn beer (6 marks)**

The starch of the corn (maize) is first changed to fermentable sugars (maltose and glucose) by the **amylase enzymes of the malt** during mashing and cooking. Then **yeast** (*Saccharomyces*) ferments the sugar anaerobically by the enzyme zymase, producing **ethanol (alcohol)** and **carbon dioxide**:

$$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} \xrightarrow{\ \text{yeast (zymase)}\ } 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 2\,\mathrm{CO_2}$$

The carbon dioxide makes the beer froth and bubble, the alcohol gives the drink its strength, and small amounts of other products (acids, esters) give flavour. The process takes place at a warm temperature for a few days, and stops when the sugar is used up or the alcohol concentration kills the yeast. The beer is then strained, and must be drunk quickly unless pasteurised or bottled.

**c.** Explain the difference between oil-in-water emulsion and water-in-oil emulsion.

(6 marks)

An **emulsion** is a mixture of two liquids that do not mix (oil and water), in which one liquid is dispersed as tiny droplets in the other; it is kept stable by an **emulsifier** (for example lecithin in egg yolk, or mustard).

| Oil-in-water (O/W) emulsion | Water-in-oil (W/O) emulsion |
|---|---|
| Tiny droplets of **oil** are spread in **water**; water is the continuous phase | Tiny droplets of **water** are spread in **oil or fat**; oil is the continuous phase |
| Contains **more water**; feels **light and watery** | Contains **more fat**; feels **greasy and rich** |
| Mixes easily with water (**can be diluted**) | Does not mix easily with water |
| Examples: milk, cream, mayonnaise, salad cream, ice cream, most sauces | Examples: butter, margarine |
| Emulsifiers: lecithin, egg yolk, casein | Emulsifiers: lecithin and monoglycerides; the fat-soluble emulsifier |

Five factors that affect food production in a Cameroonian community (2 marks each: the factor and its effect):

1. **Climate and weather:** the amount and timing of rainfall, temperature and sunshine decide what crops can grow; drought, floods and irregular rains cause crop failure.
2. **Soil fertility and land:** fertile soil gives good yields, while eroded, exhausted or acid soil gives poor yields; land shortage and land tenure problems (women often cannot own land) limit the area farmed.
3. **Capital, inputs and technology:** lack of money for improved seeds, fertiliser, tools, irrigation and machines keeps production low and traditional.
4. **Pests, diseases and post-harvest losses:** insects, rodents, fungi and animal diseases destroy crops and livestock, and poor storage and processing waste harvested food.
5. **Labour, transport, markets and government policy:** rural-urban drift of young people reduces the labour force; bad roads and poor markets discourage farmers; prices, subsidies, credit and extension services (and insecurity in some regions) can encourage or reduce production.

**a.** Identify five (5) causes of Protein Energy Malnutrition (PEM).

(5 marks)

Five causes of **Protein Energy Malnutrition** (kwashiorkor, marasmus) (1 mark each):

1. **Poverty and an inadequate diet:** too little food, or a diet lacking in protein and energy (mostly starchy foods).
2. **Poor feeding of infants:** early stopping of breastfeeding, late or poor weaning foods, and dilute or contaminated bottle feeds.
3. **Repeated infections and parasites:** diarrhoea, measles, malaria and worms reduce appetite and absorption and increase the need for protein.
4. **Ignorance and food taboos:** lack of knowledge of a balanced diet, and beliefs that forbid children from eating eggs, fish or meat.
5. **Famine, drought, war and displacement**, and **large families with closely spaced births**, so that food is shared among too many children.

**b.** Differentiate between Organic and Inorganic foods.

(8 marks)

In food science an **organic food** is food produced by **organic farming**, without synthetic fertilisers, synthetic pesticides, growth hormones, routine antibiotics or genetically modified organisms; an **inorganic** (conventional) food is produced with these inputs.

| Organic foods | Inorganic (conventionally produced) foods |
|---|---|
| Grown with **natural manure, compost** and crop rotation | Grown with **chemical (synthetic) fertilisers** |
| Pests are controlled by **natural or biological methods**, and by hand weeding | Pests and weeds are controlled with **synthetic pesticides and herbicides** |
| Animals are fed natural feed and raised without growth hormones and routine antibiotics | Animals may receive hormones, antibiotics and manufactured feeds |
| Little or **no chemical residue**; usually no artificial additives | May contain **chemical residues** and artificial additives |
| **Lower yield and higher cost**; shorter shelf life; fewer produced | **Higher yield, cheaper** and plentiful; often longer shelf life |
| Better for the soil and the environment (more biodiversity) | May harm the soil and pollute water if overused |

(In the strict chemical sense, the **organic nutrients** are those that contain carbon from living things: carbohydrates, proteins, fats and vitamins; **inorganic nutrients** are water and mineral salts.)

**c.** Suggest ways by which water can be treated to make it portable on a large scale in Cameroon.

(6 marks)

The word "portable" in the printed question is read as **potable** (safe to drink). Large-scale treatment, as done by a water company at a treatment plant (6 stages, 1 mark each):

1. **Screening and storage (sedimentation):** the raw water from a river or dam passes through screens to remove large objects, and is kept in tanks so that heavy particles settle.
2. **Coagulation and flocculation:** a chemical such as **aluminium sulphate (alum)** is added, which makes the fine suspended particles stick together into flocs that settle.
3. **Filtration:** the water passes through beds of sand and gravel (rapid or slow sand filters) that remove the remaining particles and many micro-organisms.
4. **Disinfection (chlorination):** **chlorine** (or ozone, or ultraviolet light) is added to kill disease-causing organisms (typhoid, cholera, dysentery).
5. **Aeration and pH correction:** the water is aerated to remove gases and bad taste, and the pH is corrected; fluoride may be added.
6. **Storage and distribution:** the treated water is stored in covered reservoirs and **piped** to homes, with regular testing of its quality.

(At home, small-scale treatment is by boiling, filtering and chlorine tablets.)

**d.** Plan a lunch for a strict vegetarian.

(6 marks)

A strict vegetarian eats **no meat, fish or poultry** (and a vegan also no eggs and dairy products). The lunch must still be **balanced**: energy, protein from complementary plant foods, vitamins, minerals and fibre.

| Dish | Main nutrients and role |
|---|---|
| **Boiled plantain or cooked rice** (or maize fufu) | carbohydrate: energy |
| **Beans (cowpea) stew** cooked with tomato, onion and **red palm oil** | plant **protein** (legume) which complements the cereal, iron, B vitamins, fibre; palm oil gives energy and vitamin A |
| **Sautéed green leafy vegetables** (spinach or huckleberry leaves) with groundnut paste | iron, folic acid, vitamins A and C, fibre; groundnuts add protein and fat |
| **Fruit salad** (pawpaw, orange, pineapple) | vitamin C (helps the absorption of iron from the beans and leaves), fibre and vitamins |
| **Water or fresh fruit juice** | fluid |

Points to note: cereal + legume gives **complementary protein** (all the essential amino acids); vitamin C with the iron-rich dish increases iron absorption; a strict vegan lunch should include a **vitamin B12 source** (fortified food) because B12 is found only in animal foods; the meal is cheap, colourful and uses local foods.

**a.** Who is speaking and where is the speaker? *(1+1 = 2 marks)*

**The speaker is Macbeth.** He is on the **heath** (in the open country on the way back from the battle), in **Act 1, Scene 3**, just after he has met the three witches. He speaks this passage as an aside, to himself, while the others stand near him. (1 mark for the name, 1 mark for the place.)

**b.** Name the two gentlemen to whom he gives thanks. *(2 marks)*

**Ross and Angus** (1 mark each). They are the two Scottish nobles who have come from King Duncan with news of Macbeth's reward; the extract opens with Macbeth thanking them ("I thank you, gentleman").

**c.** Give the meaning of the following words and expressions as used in the extract.

(ii) cannot be ill *(Line 6)* *(2 marks)*

(iii) unfix my hair *(Line 10)* *(2 marks)*

(iv) whose murder yet is but- fantastical *(Line 14)* *(2 marks)*

(i) **prologues**: introductions, opening parts; the first events that announce a bigger story (here, the beginning of the "imperial theme", that is, the kingship).

(ii) **cannot be ill**: cannot be evil or bad; Macbeth says the witches' prophecy cannot be a bad thing, because part of it has already come true.

(iii) **unfix my hair**: make my hair stand on end with fear or horror; the idea of murder frightens him.

(iv) **whose murder yet is but fantastical**: whose murder (the thought of killing the king) is still only imagined, in the mind, and has not been done or planned in fact.

**d.** State and explain TWO character traits of the speaker. *(2 marks)*

1. **Ambitious.** He speaks of the "swelling act / Of the imperial theme": he already sees the crown ahead, and the news that he is Thane of Cawdor makes him believe the rest of the prophecy may come true.
2. **Troubled by conscience and afraid.** The thought of murder makes his hair stand on end and his heart knock at his ribs (lines 10 to 12); he is shaken ("Shakes so my single state of man"), which shows that he knows murder would be wrong.

This matters because the witches had greeted him with this title a moment earlier. (2 marks)

Four stages, in order (2+2+2+1):

1. After his aside, Macbeth tells himself that if chance wants him to be king, chance may crown him without any action from him ("If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me, Without my stir").

3. Macbeth speaks quietly to **Banquo**, asking him to think over what has happened, so that, when there is time, they can talk openly to each other about it.
4. They all leave together to go to the King.

Three stages, in order (2 marks each):

3. At last the person is **unable to bear any more** and "ends up in institutions", broken by the struggle (line 5). (The poem does not say which institutions; do not specify further.)

6. Give a detailed account of the poem "Animals" by Walt Whitman and bring out the poet's attitude towards the subject matter. *(Detailed account = 6+6+6 = 18 marks) (Poet's attitude = 3.5+3.5 = 7 marks) (Total = 25 marks)*

**Note on method.** The poem is not printed on the paper. This answer gives the general content of the poem as it is usually known (it is the passage from Whitman's *Song of Myself* in which he praises animals); check the details against the text in the anthology before using them as a model.

**Part 1: Detailed account (18 marks, three stages of 6 marks).**

1. **The wish (6).** The speaker says that he could turn and live with animals, because they are so calm ("placid") and self-contained. He stands and looks at them for a long time.
2. **What animals do not do (6).** The speaker lists the faults of human beings that animals do not have: they do not sweat and complain about their condition; they do not lie awake in the dark weeping for their sins; they do not bother him with talk about their duty to God; none of them is unhappy with what it has, none is mad for owning things; none kneels to another, nor to others of its kind who lived thousands of years ago; none is respectable or unhappy over the whole earth.
3. **The link with the speaker (6).** The animals seem to bring him signs ("tokens") of himself; he wonders where they got them and imagines that he passed that way long ago and carelessly dropped them. The poem ends on this feeling of kinship between man and animals.

**Part 2: The poet's attitude (7 marks: 3.5+3.5).**

- **Admiration and envy**: he admires the animals' calm and contentment and wishes to live like them (3.5).
- **Criticism of human society**: he disapproves of human guilt, anxiety about religion, greed and the habit of kneeling to others, which animals are free of; at the same time he feels a close kinship with animals (3.5).

**Mark scheme (25).** Account 6/6/6 = 18; attitude 3.5/3.5 = 7.

**Common errors.** Telling only the first lines; quoting at length instead of explaining; stating the attitude without proof from the poem.

7. State and explain FIVE character traits of Jack and bring out FIVE roles he plays in the novel, *Lord of the Flies*. *(Character traits: 3+3+3+3+3 = 15 marks) (Role played: 2+2+2+2+2 = 10 marks) (Total = 25 marks)*

**Part 1: Five character traits of Jack (15 marks, 3 marks each: name, explanation, proof).**

1. **Arrogant and proud.** From the first meeting he expects to lead ("I ought to be chief", because he is the leader of the choir) and he resents Ralph's election.
2. **Hungry for power and a bully.** He cannot accept Ralph's authority, ignores the rules of the conch, and later breaks away to form his own tribe in which he rules by fear.
3. **Aggressive, cruel and bloodthirsty.** He becomes obsessed with hunting and killing pigs, paints his face, and leads the boys into savage violence, including the death of Simon and the hunt for Ralph.
4. **Brave and skilful as a hunter.** He is the one who finally kills a pig, and he leads the hunters with energy and courage.
5. **Manipulative and charismatic.** He wins the boys over with meat, feasts and the promise of protection from the "beast", which makes many of them desert Ralph.

Other acceptable traits if proved: impulsive, selfish, irresponsible about the signal fire, defiant of authority.

**Part 2: Five roles Jack plays in the novel (10 marks, 2 marks each).**

1. **Leader of the choir** at the start (head of the choirboys).
2. **Chief hunter**, who organises and leads the hunters.
3. **Ralph's rival and challenger** for leadership of the boys.
4. **Chief of the savage tribe** at Castle Rock.
5. **Symbol of savagery and of the loss of order and civilisation**, set against Ralph and Piggy, who stand for order and reason; he also leads the tribe in the violent acts of the novel, such as the attack on Ralph's group to steal Piggy's glasses.

**Mark scheme (25).** Traits 3x5 = 15; roles 2x5 = 10.

**Common errors.** Naming a trait without a proof from the story; confusing Jack with Roger or Ralph; roles that repeat the same idea.

8. Give an account of the events leading to the first assembly of the boys at the beach and state the role the Conch plays. *(Account of events: 6+6+6 = 18 marks) (Role of the Conch: 3.5+3.5 = 7 marks) (Total = 25 marks)*

**Part 1: Account of the events leading to the first assembly (18 marks, three stages of 6 marks).**

1. **The setting (6).** A group of schoolboys, being evacuated from England in wartime, survive a plane crash and find themselves alone on a tropical island, with no adults. **Ralph**, a fair-haired boy of about twelve, makes his way out of the jungle towards the lagoon and the beach.
2. **Ralph meets Piggy (6).** Near the lagoon he meets **Piggy**, a fat, short-sighted boy who wears glasses and suffers from asthma. They realise that there are no grown-ups. Piggy says that other boys must be found. A **conch shell** is found in the lagoon, and Piggy, who recognises it, explains that it can be blown like a horn to call the others together.
3. **The call (6).** Ralph blows the conch. The sound carries over the island, and the boys come out one by one, including the small children (the "littluns") and then the choir, marching in black cloaks under Jack Merridew. The boys gather on the beach, and the first assembly begins; it is there that Ralph is elected leader.

**Part 2: The role of the Conch (7 marks: 3.5+3.5).**

- **A practical tool of order (3.5):** it is blown to call the boys to assembly, and the boy who holds it has the right to speak without being interrupted, which gives the meetings order and fairness.
- **A symbol (3.5):** it stands for democracy, rules, authority and civilisation. Its power fades as the boys turn to savagery, and it is finally smashed when Piggy is killed, which marks the end of order on the island.

**Mark scheme (25).** Account 6/6/6 = 18; role of the Conch 3.5/3.5 = 7.

**Common errors.** Starting the account at the election or later; forgetting the meeting with Piggy; saying only that the conch is a shell, without its role and meaning.

**1.** A method of cooking food which involves the use of direct heat is?

a) Boiling
b) Steaming
c) Grilling
d) Poaching

Grilling cooks food by direct radiant heat from a flame, glowing coals or an electric element. Boiling, steaming and poaching cook by heat carried through water or steam (moist methods), not by direct heat.

**Answer: C.**

**2.** Deficiency of vitamin A is;

a) Rickets
b) Anaemia
c) Scurvy
d) Night blindness

Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the visual pigment of the retina, so its lack causes night blindness (and xerophthalmia). Rickets is lack of vitamin D, scurvy of vitamin C and anaemia mainly of iron, folate or vitamin B12.

**Answer: D.**

**3.** A protein that has a structural function in the body is called;

a) Albumin
b) Casein
c) Collagen
d) Gluten

Collagen is a fibrous protein that forms the structure of skin, tendons, bones and cartilage. Albumin is a transport protein of the blood, casein is the milk protein and gluten is the wheat protein.

**Answer: C.**

**4.** A man ate puff balls and beans containing 10g carbohydrates 5g of protein and 2g fats. Calculate the energy he obtained from the meal;

a) 78 kcal
b) 60 kcal
c) 58 kcal
d) 68 kcal

Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram and fat about 9 kcal per gram.

$(10 + 5)\times 4 + 2\times 9 = 60 + 18 = 78$ kcal.

Option B (60 kcal) forgets the fat.

**Answer: A.**

**5.** When testing for the presence of a non-reducing sugar, the first reagent put into the test tube is;

a) Dilute hydrochloric acid (HCL)
b) Benedict
c) Sodium hydroxide
d) Ethanol

A non-reducing sugar such as sucrose does not reduce Benedict's solution directly. The sample is first boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid to hydrolyse it into reducing sugars (glucose and fructose), then neutralised with sodium hydroxide or sodium hydrogencarbonate, and only then is Benedict's solution added and heated.

**Answer: A.**

**6.** The burette test is based on detecting the presence of;

a) Peptide bond
b) Amino acids
c) Amino group
d) Disulphide bridges

The biuret test (the printed word 'burette' is a misspelling) gives a violet colour when copper(II) ions in alkaline solution bind to the nitrogen atoms of peptide bonds. It needs at least two peptide bonds, so it detects proteins and peptides, not free amino acids.

**Answer: A.**

*Options as printed:* A) Nuts and wheat   B) Seeds and vegetable   C) Seeds and nuts   D) Fruits and seeds

Coconut is classed with nuts and seeds in food composition tables. Intended answer: C (seeds and nuts). The grouping depends on the table used (some tables use fruits and seeds).

**Intended answer: C (Seeds and nuts).**

**8.** Which enzyme in protein digestion activates the inactive form of another protein enzyme

a) Pepsin
b) Erepsin
c) Trypsin
d) Chymotrypsin

Trypsin, made as inactive trypsinogen and activated by enterokinase in the duodenum, converts chymotrypsinogen into active chymotrypsin (and activates other pancreatic zymogens). Pepsin acts in the stomach and erepsin is an old name for the peptidases of the small intestine.

**Answer: C.**

**9.** The valve that prevents regurgitation of food from the intestine back into the stomach is known as;

a) Pyloric regions
b) Cardiac sphincter
c) Fundic region
d) Pyloric sphincter

The pyloric sphincter lies between the stomach and the duodenum and controls the release of chyme into the intestine and prevents its return. The cardiac sphincter is at the oesophagus-stomach junction.

**Answer: D.**

**10.** The correct order of the movement of food in the digestive track is;

a) Duodenum, ileum, stomach, Oesophagus
b) Desophagus, stomach, Ileum, Duodenum
c) Stomach, Oesophagus, Ileum, Duodenum
d) Oesophagus, stomach, Duodenum, Ileum

Food passes oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, then ileum (the duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, the ileum the last). Option B reverses the duodenum and the ileum.

**Answer: D.**

**11.** Enzyme that changes the shape of a compound is;

a) Transferase
b) Reductase
c) Isomerase
d) Lipase

An isomerase rearranges the atoms of a molecule into an isomer (for example glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate), changing its shape. Transferases move a group, reductases add electrons or hydrogen, lipases hydrolyse fats.

**Answer: C.**

**12.** A protein that stimulates the liver to convert glycogen into glucose is called;

a) Insulin
b) Somatostatin
c) Glucagon
d) Pepsin

Glucagon, secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas when blood sugar is low, stimulates the liver to break glycogen down to glucose. Insulin does the opposite.

**Answer: C.**

*Options as printed:* A) Increase in consumption   B) Increase in importation   C) Decrease in importation   D) Price control

Intended answer: B (increase in importation). Stocks and imports both raise the quantity of food available when local production falls. Price control is also defended in some textbooks.

**Intended answer: B (Increase in importation).**

**14.** Food security could be defined as;

a) Food must be available and cheap to all people
b) Food must be available and healthy to all people
c) Food must be available all the time for all people
d) Food must be available, accessible at all time to everyone

Food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Only option D includes both availability and accessibility at all times; the others miss one of the conditions.

**Answer: D.**

a) Thrombosis
b) Angina
c) Atherosclerosis
d) Stroke

Angina pectoris is chest pain from too little blood reaching the heart muscle; it spreads to the neck and down the left arm. Thrombosis is a clot, atherosclerosis is hardening of arteries by fatty deposits and a stroke affects the brain.

**Answer: B.**

a) Artificial sacristy
b) Hoarding
c) Black marketing
d) Non availability

**Answer: B.**

b) Flavour
c) Taste
d) Appearance

b) Provides balance between rich and poor

a) Grazing
b) Greasing
c) Glazing
d) Glaze

**20.** Hyperglycemia is referred to as;

a) Increased thirst
b) Sugar in urine
c) Elevated blood sugar level
d) Increased urination

**21.** The enzyme involved in the aging and ripening of cheese is called;

a) Rennin
b) Lipase
c) Lactase
d) Amylase

Rennin (chymosin) coagulates milk protein to make curd for cheese; the proteolytic action of rennet enzymes continues during ageing and ripening. Lactase acts on lactose and amylase on starch. Lipase also acts on fat during ripening, so the question is imperfect; rennin is the standard textbook answer.

**22.** Identify an enzyme inhibitor from below;

a) Sulphurnamides
b) Flavine Adenine Dinucleotide
c) Haem
d) Chloride ions

Sulphonamides (printed 'sulphurnamides') resemble para-aminobenzoic acid and compete for the active site of the bacterial enzyme that makes folic acid, so they are competitive inhibitors. FAD and haem are coenzyme or prosthetic groups and chloride ions are activators of amylase.

a) Beer
b) Spirit
c) Wine
d) Cider

Beer usually contains about 4-6 percent alcohol. Wine has about 10-14 percent and spirits about 40 percent. Cider has about 4-8 percent, so the question is slightly loose, but beer is the standard answer.

**a.** Differentiate between the following words giving examples each:

(i) Glazing and Grazing (4 marks)

(ii) Bouquet-garni and Roux. (4 marks)

**(i) Glazing and grazing (4 marks)**

| Glazing | Grazing |
|---|---|
| Coating the surface of a food with a thin shiny layer (a glaze) to improve its appearance, flavour or protection. | Eating small amounts of food (snacks) frequently through the day instead of taking regular main meals. |
| Example: brushing beaten egg or milk over pastry or bread before baking; brushing a cake with sugar syrup or apricot jam; coating carrots with butter and sugar. | Example: nibbling fruit, groundnuts, biscuits or plantain chips every hour or so while working. |

**(ii) Bouquet-garni and roux (4 marks)**

| Bouquet-garni | Roux |
|---|---|
| A small bundle of fresh herbs (for example parsley stalks, thyme and a bay leaf) tied together or put in a muslin bag, used to flavour soups, stews and sauces, and removed before serving. | A cooked mixture of equal weights of fat (butter or margarine) and flour, used to thicken sauces and soups. |
| Example: added to a pot of vegetable soup or beef stew. | Example: the base of white sauce (cheese sauce, parsley sauce); it may be white, blond or brown depending on how long it is cooked. |

**b.** Explain using the following; requirements, procedure, observation and conclusion, the test for starch. (6 marks)

**Test for starch (iodine test)**

- **Requirements:** the food sample (for example cooked cassava, potato or flour paste), a white tile or a test tube, a dropper, distilled water, and iodine solution (iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution).
- **Procedure:** 1. Place a small amount of the food on a white tile (a solid), or mix a little of it with water in a test tube. 2. Add 2 to 3 drops of iodine solution to the sample. 3. Observe the colour at once.
- **Observation:** the iodine solution changes from brown (yellow-brown) to a blue-black (deep blue or purple-black) colour.
- **Conclusion:** starch is present in the food. If the colour stays brown or orange-yellow, starch is absent.

(Marks: requirements 1.5, procedure 1.5, observation 1.5, conclusion 1.5.)

**c.** Enumerate the functions of proteins in the body. (5 marks)

Functions of proteins in the body (1 mark each, any five):

1. **Growth and development** of the body: they build new cells and tissues, especially in children, adolescents and pregnant women.
2. **Repair and maintenance** of worn-out or damaged cells and tissues (for example healing of wounds).
3. **Enzymes and hormones:** many enzymes (for example pepsin, amylase) and hormones (for example insulin) are proteins that control body reactions.
4. **Antibodies:** proteins that defend the body against infections and form part of immunity.
5. **Transport:** for example haemoglobin carries oxygen and plasma proteins carry substances in the blood.
6. **Source of energy:** when carbohydrates and fats are lacking, 1 g of protein yields about 17 kJ (4 kcal).
7. **Fluid balance and blood clotting:** plasma proteins maintain water balance, and fibrinogen is needed for clotting.
8. **Structure:** keratin forms hair and nails, collagen forms skin, bone and cartilage; muscle proteins (actin, myosin) allow movement.

**d.** Calculate the body mass index (BMI) of a 38 year old soldier who weighs 80kg and has a height of 1.87m and state his nutritional status. (6 marks)

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}$$

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{80}{1.87^2} = \frac{80}{3.4969} = 22.88\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}} \approx 22.9\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}}$$

**Nutritional status:** the normal (healthy) range for an adult is a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9. Since 22.9 lies in this range, the soldier has a **normal nutritional status** (he is neither underweight nor overweight). The BMI is a general guide only: a muscular soldier could have a high BMI without being overfat.

**a.** (i) Explain the term 'Recommended Dietary Allowance' (RDA). (2 marks)

**a.** (i) Explain the term 'Recommended Dietary Allowance' (RDA). (2 marks)

(ii) Describe two (2) factors that will affect recommended dietary allowance (RDA). (4 marks)

**(i)** The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is the average daily amount of a nutrient (energy, protein, vitamins, minerals) that is enough to meet the needs of almost all (about 97 to 98 per cent) healthy people of a given age, sex and physiological group.

**(ii)** Two factors (2 marks each: naming 1 + description 1):

1. **Age:** growing children and adolescents need more protein, calcium and iron per kilogram of body weight than adults, because of rapid growth; older people need less energy because their metabolism slows down.
2. **Physiological state:** pregnant and breast-feeding women need extra energy, protein, iron, folic acid and calcium for the baby and for milk production.

(Other acceptable factors: sex, body size and weight, occupation and level of physical activity, climate, state of health or disease.)

**b.** Enumerate five (5) uses of the Food Composition Table (FCT). (5 marks)

Uses of the Food Composition Table (1 mark each, any five):

1. To find the **nutrient content** (energy, protein, fat, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals) of a given quantity of a food.
2. To **calculate the nutritional value** of a meal or of a whole day's diet.
3. To **plan balanced meals and diets** that meet the RDA of a person or group.
4. To **compare foods** and choose the best source of a nutrient (for example the richest source of iron).
5. To plan **therapeutic (special) diets** for patients, for example diabetic or low-salt diets.
6. To assess the **nutritional status** of a community through food intake surveys.
7. To help in **food labelling, food processing and food policy** (planning food production and supplies), and in nutrition education and research.

**c.** State and explain two (2) effect of heat on proteins. (4 marks)

Two effects of heat on proteins (2 marks each: statement 1 + explanation 1):

1. **Denaturation and coagulation.** Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the protein molecule in shape, so it unfolds and the proteins stick together and set. Example: egg white changes from clear and runny to white and solid; the flesh of meat and fish becomes firm.
2. **Shrinkage, loss of water and hardening (toughening).** Prolonged or very high heat makes the coagulated protein contract and squeeze out water, so the food becomes tough, dry and harder to digest. Example: an overcooked egg or overcooked meat becomes rubbery.

(Other acceptable effects: browning by the Maillard reaction when proteins and sugars are heated together gives colour and flavour; gelatinisation of collagen (heat and moisture change collagen to gelatine and tenderise tough meat); loss of some nutritive value (lysine) with excessive heat; killing of micro-organisms.)

**d.** John`s diet provides a total of 2200Kcal of energy of which 40% is from fat and 20% from proteins. How many grams of carbohydrates are contained in the diet? (10 marks)

**Step 1: percentage from carbohydrate.** $100 - (40 + 20) = 40\%$ of the energy comes from carbohydrate.

**Step 2: energy from carbohydrate.** $\dfrac{40}{100} \times 2200 = 880\ \mathrm{kcal}$

**Step 3: convert to grams.** 1 g of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal:

$$\text{mass of carbohydrate} = \frac{880}{4} = 220\ \mathrm{g}$$

**Answer: the diet contains about 220 g of carbohydrate.**

(Check: fat $= 0.40 \times 2200 = 880\ \mathrm{kcal} = 97.8\ \mathrm{g}$ at 9 kcal g$^{-1}$; protein $= 0.20 \times 2200 = 440\ \mathrm{kcal} = 110\ \mathrm{g}$ at 4 kcal g$^{-1}$; $880 + 440 + 880 = 2200$ kcal.)

**SECTION B**

**a.** Give any three nutrients that are absorbed in the large intestines. (3 marks)

**b.** Describe the absorption and transportation of fatty acids into the blood stream. (8 marks)

**a.** Give any three nutrients that are absorbed in the large intestines. (3 marks)

Nutrients absorbed in the large intestine (1 mark each, any three):

1. **Water** (most of the remaining water is reabsorbed there).
2. **Mineral salts (electrolytes)**, especially sodium and chloride ions (and some potassium).
3. **Vitamins made by bacteria** in the colon: vitamin K and some B vitamins (for example biotin and B12).
4. **Short-chain fatty acids** produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fibre (a small amount of energy).

**b.** Describe the absorption and transportation of fatty acids into the blood stream. (8 marks)

**Absorption and transport of fatty acids**

1. Fats are emulsified by **bile salts** and digested by **pancreatic and intestinal lipase** in the small intestine into **fatty acids and monoglycerides** (glycerol and fatty acids).
2. The fatty acids and monoglycerides join with bile salts to form tiny **micelles**, which carry them to the surface of the epithelial cells of the **villi** of the small intestine.
3. They are **absorbed by diffusion** across the cell membrane (they dissolve in the lipid membrane).
4. Inside the epithelial cells they are **re-synthesised into triglycerides**, which are coated with protein to form tiny droplets called **chylomicrons**.
5. The chylomicrons are too large to enter the blood capillaries directly, so they pass into the **lacteal** (lymph capillary) in the centre of each villus.
6. They are carried in the **lymph** through the lymphatic vessels to the **thoracic duct**, which empties into the **subclavian vein**, so they enter the blood stream.
7. In the blood, the enzyme **lipoprotein lipase** breaks chylomicrons down so that fatty acids can enter the cells; the remnants go to the liver.
8. Short-chain fatty acids and glycerol, being water soluble, may instead pass directly into the blood capillaries and go to the liver by the hepatic portal vein.

**c.** Explain the fate of absorbed lipids in the body. (4 marks)

Fate of absorbed lipids (1 mark each, any four with explanation):

1. **Oxidised for energy:** fatty acids are broken down in the cells (and in the liver) to release energy; 1 g of fat gives about 37 kJ (9 kcal).
2. **Stored as adipose tissue:** excess fat is stored under the skin and around organs as an energy reserve, as insulation against heat loss and as protection (cushion) for organs.
3. **Structural use:** phospholipids and cholesterol are built into cell membranes and nerve sheaths.
4. **Synthesis of other compounds:** cholesterol is used to make steroid hormones, vitamin D and bile salts; fats carry and help absorb the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
5. **Converted by the liver** into lipoproteins for transport, or into carbohydrate/other compounds when needed.

**d.** Explain five (5) points to consider when buying large quantity of a commodity at a time. (10 marks)

Points to consider when buying a large quantity of a commodity (2 marks each: point 1 + explanation 1; any five):

1. **Money available (budget).** Large purchases tie up money, so check that it will not prevent paying for other essential needs.
2. **Storage space and conditions.** There must be enough clean, dry, cool, rodent- and insect-proof space (or refrigeration/freezer) to keep the goods.
3. **Keeping quality (perishability).** Perishable foods such as fresh fish or vegetables will spoil before being used; non-perishable foods such as rice, sugar and tinned foods can be bought in bulk.
4. **Price and discount.** Compare unit prices; buying in bulk is worthwhile only if the saving is real (wholesale price, discount, seasonal low price).
5. **Quality and date marking.** Check the quality, brand, packaging, and expiry or 'best before' date so that the food will be used in time.
6. **Number of people and rate of consumption.** The quantity should match what the family or institution will actually use, to avoid waste.
7. **Reliability of the supplier and transport.** Choose a trusted seller and consider how the goods will be carried home.

**(ii) Entrepreneur:** a person who identifies a business opportunity, organises the resources (land, labour, capital), starts and manages the enterprise, and takes the risk of making a profit or a loss. Example: a woman who starts a small business producing and selling fruit juice or dried fish.

**c.** Explain the term "sensory evaluation" (3 marks)

**Sensory evaluation** is the scientific method of measuring, analysing and interpreting people's reactions to the characteristics of a food as perceived by the senses: **appearance (sight), smell (aroma), taste, texture or feel (touch, mouthfeel) and sound** (for example crispness). **a.** Differentiate between a preference test and a discrimination test, give an example of each test. (4 marks)

| Preference (affective) test | Discrimination (difference) test |
|---|---|
| Finds out which sample, or how much, consumers **like or prefer** (personal choice and acceptability). | Finds out whether panellists can **detect a difference** between samples (or identify the odd one), without asking which one they like. |
| Uses untrained consumer panels, often large. | Uses trained or screened panellists. |
| Example: paired preference test or hedonic scale, where panellists say which of two biscuits (or fruit juices) they prefer or score it from 'like very much' to 'dislike very much'. | Example: triangle test (three samples, two the same, panellists pick the odd one) or duo-trio test, used for instance to see if a change of sugar or recipe can be detected. |

**b.** State the importance of sensory evaluation in the food processing industry. (5 marks)

Importance of sensory evaluation in the food processing industry (1 mark each, any five):

1. It helps in the **development of new products** by testing how consumers react to them.
2. It is used to **improve existing products** (taste, colour, texture) by testing changes in recipe or ingredients.
3. It is used for **quality control**, to check that every batch has the same quality and to detect faults (off-flavours).
4. It helps to **assess consumer acceptance and preference**, and so to predict the success of a product on the market.
5. It is used to **compare products** with those of competitors and to choose the best formulation.
6. It helps to **judge the effect of processing, packaging and storage** (shelf life) on the sensory quality of food.
7. It guides the choice of a **cheaper ingredient or process** without loss of quality, and in setting standards and grades.

**c.** Classify enzymes based on the type of reaction they catalyse, giving an example in each class. (12 marks)

Enzymes are grouped into six classes according to the type of reaction they catalyse (2 marks each: class + reaction 1, example 1):

| Class | Reaction catalysed | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. **Oxidoreductases** | Oxidation-reduction reactions: transfer of electrons or hydrogen from one substance to another | Alcohol dehydrogenase; polyphenol oxidase (browning of cut fruit); glucose oxidase |
| 2. **Transferases** | Transfer of a functional group (for example amino or phosphate group) from one molecule to another | Transaminase; hexokinase |
| 3. **Hydrolases** | Breaking of bonds by addition of water (hydrolysis) | Amylase (starch to maltose); lipase (fat to fatty acids and glycerol); protease such as pepsin; lactase |
| 4. **Lyases** | Removal of a group from a substance (or addition to a double bond) without hydrolysis, forming a double bond | Pyruvate decarboxylase (pyruvate to ethanal and carbon dioxide); fumarase |
| 5. **Isomerases** | Rearrangement of atoms within a molecule (conversion of one isomer into another) | Glucose isomerase (glucose to fructose); phosphoglucose isomerase |
| 6. **Ligases (synthetases)** | Joining of two molecules using energy from ATP | DNA ligase; pyruvate carboxylase |

**d.** Define glycolysis and explain its role in alcohol fermentation. (4 marks)

**Glycolysis** is the series of enzyme-controlled reactions in the cytoplasm of the cell in which one molecule of glucose (6 carbons) is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate (3 carbons), with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 reduced NAD (NADH). It does not need oxygen.

**Role in alcohol fermentation:** in the absence of oxygen (for example in yeast), glycolysis is the only energy-releasing stage. The pyruvate is then decarboxylated to ethanal (releasing carbon dioxide), and ethanal is reduced to ethanol by the NADH, which is changed back to NAD. This regeneration of NAD allows glycolysis to continue, so that the yeast keeps producing 2 ATP per glucose. The products are ethanol and carbon dioxide (used in brewing, wine making and to raise bread dough).

**a.** Differentiate between oil-in-water (o/w) and water-in-oil (w/o) Emulsions. (6 marks)

**a.** Differentiate between oil-in-water (o/w) and water-in-oil (w/o) Emulsions. (6 marks)

An **emulsion** is a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix (oil and water), in which one is dispersed as tiny droplets in the other, usually with the help of an emulsifier.

| Oil-in-water (o/w) emulsion | Water-in-oil (w/o) emulsion |
|---|---|
| Tiny droplets of **oil** are dispersed in a continuous phase of **water**. | Tiny droplets of **water** are dispersed in a continuous phase of **oil**. |
| Feels light and not greasy; easily diluted with water. | Feels greasy and heavy; not diluted with water. |
| Emulsifiers that dissolve better in water (for example egg yolk lecithin, casein) are used. | Emulsifiers that dissolve better in oil are used. |
| Examples: milk, mayonnaise, salad cream, cream, ice cream. | Examples: butter, margarine. |

**b.** Explain four (4) factors that influence the stability of emulsions. (8 marks)

Factors that influence the stability of emulsions (2 marks each: factor 1 + explanation 1; any four):

1. **Presence and type of emulsifier.** An emulsifier (lecithin, proteins, gums) forms a film round each droplet and lowers surface tension, so droplets do not join (coalesce); without it the emulsion separates.
2. **Size of the droplets.** Smaller droplets (for example by homogenisation or vigorous whisking) stay suspended longer and make a more stable emulsion.
3. **Temperature.** High heat lowers viscosity and may denature the protein emulsifier, causing separation (curdling of mayonnaise); freezing can break the emulsion; a cool, steady temperature keeps it stable.
4. **Viscosity of the continuous phase.** A thick continuous phase (added gums, starch or sugar) slows the movement of droplets, so the emulsion stays stable.
5. **Proportion of the two phases / rate of addition.** Too much of the dispersed phase, or adding oil too quickly, overloads the emulsifier and breaks the emulsion.
6. **pH and presence of salts (electrolytes).** Changes in acidity or too much salt can upset the charge on the emulsifier and make droplets join.
7. **Agitation and time.** Strong shaking after formation or long storage encourages separation.

**c.** Expatiate on three (3) uses of Enzymes in a food industry. (6 marks)

Uses of enzymes in the food industry (2 marks each: use 1 + explanation 1; any three):

1. **Brewing and baking.** Amylase converts starch to sugars (maltose), which yeast ferments to alcohol and carbon dioxide in brewing, and to raise bread dough (better volume and crust colour).
2. **Cheese making.** Rennet (rennin, chymosin) clots milk protein (casein) to form the curd that is made into cheese; lipases add flavour.
3. **Fruit juice clarification.** Pectinases break down pectin, so that more juice is released and the juice becomes clear.
4. **Meat tenderising.** Papain (from pawpaw) and bromelain (from pineapple) break down tough muscle proteins.
5. **Syrup and sweetener production.** Amylases and glucose isomerase convert starch to glucose and then fructose (high-fructose syrup).
6. **Dairy products.** Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose to make lactose-free milk.

**d.** Discuss five (5) ways by which food can be preserved in your community. (5 marks)

Ways of preserving food in the community (1 mark each, with a short explanation):

1. **Drying (sun drying):** fish, meat, cassava, maize, vegetables and pepper are dried in the sun or on a rack; removing water stops micro-organisms from growing.
2. **Smoking:** fish and meat are placed over a wood fire; heat dries them and smoke chemicals kill or slow micro-organisms.
3. **Salting:** salt draws water out by osmosis, so bacteria cannot multiply (used for fish and meat).
4. **Refrigeration and freezing:** low temperature slows or stops the growth of micro-organisms and enzymes; used where electricity is available.
5. **Boiling/cooking and reheating:** heat destroys micro-organisms, so food (for example soups, stews, milk) keeps longer.
6. **Using sugar, oil or vinegar (pickling and jam making):** high sugar or acid concentration prevents spoilage; palm oil or other oil is also used to cover foods.
7. **Canning and bottling** (in some households and industries).

**a.** Which strategies that could be put in place to ensure safe water supply to a community? (5 marks)

Strategies to ensure a safe water supply to a community (1 mark each, any five):

1. **Protect water sources** (springs, wells, rivers, catchment areas) from pollution by fencing them and keeping latrines, farms, waste and animals away.
2. **Provide treated piped water** through a water treatment plant (sedimentation, filtration, chlorination) and a distribution network, with regular maintenance.
3. **Construct protected wells, boreholes and stand-pipes** with covers, lining and a clean surround.
4. **Test water regularly** (chemical and bacteriological tests) to confirm that it is safe.
5. **Educate the community** on water hygiene: boiling or filtering drinking water, covering water containers and washing hands.
6. **Proper waste and sewage disposal** to avoid contamination of water, and enactment and enforcement of laws against water pollution.
7. **Collect and store rain water** in clean covered tanks, and form water management committees to look after the water points.

**b.** Briefly explain how water from a well could be treated for home consumption? (5 marks)

Treating well water for home use (1 mark each step with a short explanation):

1. **Sedimentation:** leave the water in a covered container for some hours so that the heavy particles settle; pour the clear water off.
2. **Filtration:** pass the water through a clean cloth or a sand, gravel and charcoal filter to remove the remaining dirt and some micro-organisms.
3. **Boiling:** boil the water vigorously for at least 5 to 10 minutes to kill disease-causing micro-organisms (bacteria, viruses, protozoa); let it cool in a clean covered container.
4. **Chlorination (or other disinfection):** add the correct amount of chlorine (bleach or chlorine tablets) and leave it for about 30 minutes; sunlight (solar disinfection) can also be used.
5. **Storage:** keep the treated water in a clean, covered container with a tap or a clean ladle, to avoid recontamination.

**c.** As a food science student, which advice can you give to a diabetic patient to improve his/her health? (7 marks)

Advice to a diabetic patient (1 mark each, any seven):

1. **Take regular, balanced meals** at fixed times and avoid skipping meals.
2. **Avoid or limit sugar and sugary foods** (sweets, soft drinks, cakes, honey, sweetened juices).
3. **Choose complex carbohydrates** with a low glycaemic index (whole grains, beans, unpeeled root crops) in controlled portions, because they release sugar slowly.
4. **Eat plenty of fibre**: vegetables, fruits and legumes slow the absorption of glucose.
5. **Reduce saturated fats and salt** (fried and fatty foods) to protect the heart and blood pressure; prefer vegetable oils in small amounts.
6. **Keep to a healthy body weight** and lose weight if overweight.
7. **Take regular exercise** (for example walking 30 minutes a day), which lowers blood sugar.
8. **Take the medicine or insulin as prescribed**, check blood sugar regularly and attend clinic visits.
9. **Avoid alcohol and smoking**, care for the feet and eyes, and see a doctor if symptoms such as great thirst or frequent urination appear.

**d.** State four (4) consequences of too much alcohol consumption in a community. (8 marks)

Consequences of too much alcohol consumption (2 marks each: consequence 1 + explanation 1; any four):

1. **Health problems:** liver damage (cirrhosis), stomach ulcers, high blood pressure, heart disease, damage to the brain and nerves, and malnutrition because alcohol replaces food and prevents absorption of vitamins (especially B vitamins).
2. **Accidents and violence:** drunken people cause road accidents, fights, crime and injuries.
3. **Family and social problems:** quarrels, child neglect, broken homes, poverty because money is spent on drink instead of food, school fees and health care.
4. **Economic loss:** reduced productivity, absenteeism and loss of jobs; the community spends on treatment and policing.
5. **Addiction and mental problems:** alcoholism, depression, loss of self-control and early death.
6. **Birth problems:** pregnant women who drink may give birth to babies with defects (foetal alcohol syndrome).

**a.** Define the term "community" giving an example. (3 marks)

A **community** is a group of people who live in the same place or area (a village, town or neighbourhood), share common interests, services and facilities (such as water, a market, a school, a health centre) and often a common culture and way of life, and who interact with one another.

Example: a village such as Bambui, or a neighbourhood in Bamenda or Douala, with its people, school, market and health centre.

**b.** Differentiate between hard and soft water. (6 marks)

| Hard water | Soft water |
|---|---|
| Contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts (hydrogencarbonates, sulphates, chlorides). | Contains few or no dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. |
| Does not form lather easily with soap; forms scum. | Forms lather easily with soap; no scum. |
| Forms scale (fur) in kettles, boilers and pipes. | Does not form scale. |
| Examples: water from wells, boreholes and springs in limestone or chalk areas. | Examples: rain water, distilled water, water from some rivers on granite or sandy soils. |
| Foods such as beans and vegetables cook more slowly and may be tougher; tea tastes less good. | Food cooks faster; tea and coffee taste better. |
| **Temporary hardness** (hydrogencarbonates) is removed by boiling; **permanent hardness** (sulphates, chlorides) needs chemical softening (washing soda, ion exchange). | Needs no treatment for hardness. |

**c.** State and explain five (5) factors that will influence food habit. (10 marks)

Factors that influence food habits (2 marks each: factor 1 + explanation 1; any five):

1. **Culture, tradition and religion.** People eat the foods of their ethnic group and avoid forbidden ones (for example no pork for Muslims; special dishes at feasts and ceremonies).
2. **Availability of food (climate, geography and season).** People eat what is grown or sold in their area and in season (for example plantain, cassava and fish in the humid south, millet and sorghum in the north).
3. **Income (economic status) and cost.** A low income limits the choice to cheaper foods; a higher income allows more meat, fish and imported foods.
4. **Education and nutrition knowledge.** Knowledge of the value of foods leads people to choose balanced diets.
5. **Age, sex, health and occupation.** Children, the sick, pregnant women and manual workers eat different amounts and kinds of food; food allergies or diseases (for example diabetes) change what is eaten.
6. **Advertising, media and food fashions.** Advertising and the influence of friends can change what people eat (fast food, soft drinks).
7. **Food preparation skills, time and facilities** (fuel, equipment, storage) available in the household; personal likes and dislikes.

**d.** Explain the function of any three (3) population groups in the community. (6 marks)

Population groups and their functions in a community (2 marks each: group 1 + function 1; any three):

1. **Children (infants and school children):** they are the future of the community; they need to be protected, fed and educated so that they grow into healthy productive adults and later replace the old.
2. **Youths (adolescents and young adults):** they supply labour and energy for farming, trade and development, bring new ideas, and are the future parents and leaders.
3. **Adults (men and women of working age):** they produce food and income, take care of the young and the old, pay taxes and make decisions and laws for the community.
4. **Women (mothers):** they bear and raise children, prepare food for the family and often farm and trade, so they are key to the nutrition and health of the household.
5. **The elderly:** they give advice, pass on culture, traditions and skills, help settle disputes and look after young children.
6. **Vulnerable groups** (pregnant and nursing mothers, the sick, the disabled): the community must give them special care and food; they are the target of health and nutrition programmes.

**6.** King Duncan says, "The love that follows us sometime is our trouble, which still we thank as love." This statement is a good example of:

*Options as printed:* A) Irony   B) Metaphor   C) Simile   D) Oxymoron

Duncan speaks these words to Lady Macbeth when he arrives at Inverness (Act 1 Scene 6). He says that the love of his subjects sometimes puts them to trouble, yet he thanks them for it as love. There is no "like" or "as" comparison, so it is not a simile, and the sentence does not set two opposite words side by side in one phrase in the way an oxymoron does. Irony, paradox or a loose metaphor can each be argued, and the printed options do not separate them safely. The line is also ironic in the play because Duncan is welcomed by the very people who will kill him.

**a.** (i) Identify the speaker and the person being addressed? *(1+1 = 2 marks)*

(ii) Where are they? *(1 mark)*

(i) The speaker is **Lady Macbeth**. In the first line ("Give him tending") she speaks to the **messenger** who has brought news; from "Come, you spirits" she addresses the **evil spirits** ("you murdering ministers") and then "thick night", which she calls on to help her.

(ii) They are at **Macbeth's castle at Inverness**, where King Duncan is about to arrive (the extract itself speaks of "my battlements").

**b.** What has provoked the speech above? *(3 marks)*

The speech is provoked by **the news that King Duncan is coming to Macbeth's castle that very night** ("the fatal entrance of Duncan / Under my battlements"). Lady Macbeth had just read her husband's letter about the witches' prophecies; the messenger's news gives her the chance to have Duncan killed under her own roof, so she calls on the spirits to harden her and to give her the cruelty she needs to carry out the murder.

**c.** Explain the following words and expressions as used in the extract.

(i) battlements *(Line 5)* *(2 marks)*

(ii) direst cruelty *(Line 8)* *(2 marks)*

(iii) compunctious *(Line 10)* *(2 marks)*

(iv) pall *(Line 16)* *(2 marks)*

(i) **battlements**: the walls at the top of a castle, with openings to shoot from; here, the castle itself.

(ii) **direst cruelty**: the most terrible, dreadful cruelty; Lady Macbeth asks to be filled with total, merciless cruelty.

(iii) **compunctious**: full of guilt or pity; "compunctious visitings of nature" are the feelings of pity and conscience that come naturally to a human being and might stop her.

(iv) **pall**: to cover or wrap, as with a dark cloth; she asks the night to wrap itself in the thickest smoke of hell.

**d.** Pick and name one figure of speech and bring out its effectiveness as used in the extract. *(1+1+1 = 3 marks)*

Any one, named, quoted and explained:

- **Apostrophe / personification**: "Come, you spirits ... Come, thick night" - she speaks to spirits and to the night as if they were persons who can hear her. **Effect**: it shows her fierce will and makes the scene dark and supernatural; she asks the forces of evil to take over her nature.
- **Metaphor**: "take my milk for gall" (gall is bitter poison) - **Effect**: it shows she wants to lose all tenderness and kindness and be filled with bitterness.
- **Imagery**: "the blanket of the dark" - **Effect**: the night becomes a cover that hides the crime even from heaven.
- **Repetition**: "Come ... Come ..." - **Effect**: it builds urgency and determination.

**e.** Give an account of the rest of the scene. *(2+2+2+2 = 8 marks)*

This is Act 1, Scene 5. In the rest of the scene:

1. **Macbeth arrives** at the castle and Lady Macbeth greets him warmly, calling him "Great Glamis! worthy Cawdor!", recalling the witches' greetings.
2. She tells him that his letter has made her feel "the future in the instant".
3. Macbeth tells her that **Duncan comes here tonight**. She asks when he will leave, and Macbeth answers "Tomorrow, as he purposes"; she replies that the sun will never see that morrow.
4. She advises him to hide his thoughts, to "look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under 't", and to welcome the king with a friendly face.
5. She takes charge of the plan: "Leave all the rest to me", and Macbeth says they will speak more of it later.

(i) **hell-gate**: the gate of hell; the Porter jokes that Macbeth's castle is like hell, so he is the keeper of hell's gate.

**SECTION C: POETRY. HANS BOKWE ITOE: MODERN ANTHOLOGY OF POETRY**

**a.** Give a detailed account of the poem "Down by the Salley Gardens" by W. B. Yeats. *(Detailed account 9+9 = 18 marks)*

**b.** Bring out the poet's attitude towards the subject matter and the moral lessons learnt from the poem. *(Poet's attitude 3.5 marks; Moral lessons 3.5 marks; total 7 marks)*

**a.** Give a detailed account of the poem "Down by the Salley Gardens" by W. B. Yeats. *(Detailed account 9+9 = 18 marks)*

"Down by the Salley Gardens" is a **short love poem in two stanzas** ("salley" means willow); the speaker, a young man, looks back on a lost love.

**Stanza 1.** The speaker remembers that he and his love **met down by the salley gardens**, where she passed by "with little snow-white feet". She **told him to take love easy, "as the leaves grow on the tree"** (calmly, naturally, patiently). **But he, being young and foolish, did not agree** with her.

**Stanza 2.** The speaker recalls that they **stood together in a field by the river**, and she laid her snow-white hand on his leaning shoulder. She advised him to **take life easy, "as the grass grows on the weirs"** (the grass on the river banks grows slowly and quietly). **But again he was young and foolish, and now he is "full of tears"** because he has lost her.

The poem moves from a **happy memory** to a **sad present**: the two stanzas have the same pattern (the place, the girl's advice, the speaker's refusal), which shows the speaker repeating the same mistake and now regretting it.

**b.** Bring out the poet's attitude towards the subject matter and the moral lessons learnt from the poem. *(Poet's attitude 3.5 marks; Moral lessons 3.5 marks; total 7 marks)*

**Poet's attitude**: the poet (speaker) is **nostalgic, regretful and sorrowful**. He looks back with tenderness on the girl and the places they met, but he blames his own youth and foolishness ("I was young and foolish") for the loss. The last line ("now am full of tears") shows deep sadness and self-reproach.

**Moral lessons**:
1. **Take love and life patiently**, letting them grow naturally "as the leaves grow on the tree", without haste or force.
2. **Listen to good advice** from those who love and know us; ignoring it leads to regret.
3. **Youthful pride or rashness can cost a person happiness**: foolish decisions made when young may be regretted for life.

**a.** State and explain FIVE character traits of Jack Merridew. *(Character trait: 3+3+3+3+3 = 15 marks)*

Five traits, each named, explained and supported from the novel (3 marks each):

1. **Arrogant and domineering**: Jack arrives as the leader of the choir and expects to be chief; he cannot accept Ralph being elected.
2. **Obsessed with hunting and violence**: his main aim becomes killing a pig; he is ready to be cruel for the thrill of the hunt.
3. **Power-hungry and jealous**: he challenges Ralph, quarrels with him in the assemblies and finally breaks away to form his own tribe.
4. **Manipulative, a leader who rules by fear**: he uses the fear of the beast to control the boys, and he rewards followers with meat and feasts.
5. **Savage and cruel**: with his face painted, he loses all restraint; his hunters take part in the killing of Simon, the theft of Piggy's glasses and the hunt for Ralph.

(Other acceptable traits if explained: charismatic, proud, irresponsible about the fire, ruthless.)

**b.** State and explain FIVE roles he plays in the events of the novel. *(Role played: 2+2+2+2+2 = 10 marks)*

Five roles, each named and shown in an event (2 marks each):

1. **Leader of the choir and the hunters**: he organises the choirboys into a hunting group.
2. **Hunter and provider of meat**: he finally kills a pig, which gives the boys meat and changes their attitude towards him.
3. **Rival to Ralph**: he opposes Ralph's authority, disputes his rules and divides the boys.
4. **Founder and chief of a rival tribe**: he leaves Ralph's group and leads his own tribe at Castle Rock, where he rules as a tyrant.
5. **Destroyer of order and civilisation**: his hunters let the signal fire die out, take part in the killing of Simon, steal Piggy's glasses and, at the end, hunt Ralph, setting the island on fire; he thus brings the island to savagery until the naval officer arrives.

**a.** Give a DETAILED ACCOUNT of the second meeting convened by Ralph, held after the expedition. *(Detailed Account 6+6+6 = 18 marks)*

This is the **second assembly**, which Ralph calls on the beach **after the boys have explored the island** (the expedition up the mountain by Ralph, Jack and Simon). An account in three stages (6 marks each):

1. **Opening**: Ralph blows the **conch** to call the boys together and tells them what he has found: they are on an **island with no grown-ups**. He says they must be rescued and that they **need rules**.
2. **The rules and the fire**: he explains that **whoever holds the conch has the right to speak** and must not be interrupted; Jack agrees that there must be rules ("We'll have rules!") and says the hunters will hunt. Ralph says the most important thing is **to make a smoke signal on the mountain** to attract ships; the boys build a fire with Piggy's glasses and the fire gets out of hand.
3. **Fear and disorder**: a small boy talks about **a "beastie" or snake-thing he saw in the dark**, which alarms the others; Ralph says there is no beast, but the meeting becomes noisy. The fire spreads over the mountain, and it is realised that **one of the small boys is missing**, which shows the first danger from their carelessness.

(Details and their order should be checked against the novel.)

**b.** Bring out THREE importance of the use of the Conch in the meeting. *(Importance of the Conch 2+2+2+1 = 7 marks)*

Three importances (2 marks each), plus a closing point (1 mark):

1. **It gives the right to speak**: whoever holds the conch is allowed to speak, and the others must listen, which stops the boys from all shouting together.
2. **It is the symbol of order, democracy and authority**: the conch stands for Ralph's leadership and for the rules the boys have agreed to follow.
3. **It is used to call the boys together**: its sound summons the assembly and so gathers the group under one authority.

**Closing point (1 mark)**: the conch is the **symbol of civilisation** on the island; the way the boys respect it at first, and ignore it later, measures their slide into savagery.

**a.** (i) Who is speaking and to whom? *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

**a.** (i) Who is speaking and to whom? *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

(ii) Where are they? *(1 mark)*

(i) The speaker is **Rosalind** (disguised as the young man Ganymede), and she is speaking to **Phebe**, the proud shepherdess who has just scorned Silvius.

(ii) They are in the **Forest of Arden**, in the open country where the shepherds live.

**b.** Who is the foolish shepherd addressed in this manner? *(2 marks)*

The foolish shepherd is **Silvius**, the lovesick shepherd who follows Phebe and begs her to love him. Rosalind calls him foolish because he runs after a woman who does not deserve his love.

**c.** What prompted the speaker to speak in this manner? *(2 marks)*

Rosalind had been watching, unseen, while **Phebe treated Silvius with pride and scorn** and refused his love in cruel words. Angry at Phebe's cruelty and at Silvius's helplessness, Rosalind comes forward and scolds Phebe: she tells her that she is not beautiful enough to be so proud, and that she should be grateful for a good man's love.

**d.** Give the meaning of the following words and expressions as used in the extract.

(i) Exult *(Line 3)* *(2 marks)*

(ii) The ordinary *(Line 4)* *(2 marks)*

(iii) Inky brows *(Line 8)* *(2 marks)*

(iv) Properer *(Line 11)* *(2 marks)*

(i) **exult**: to rejoice proudly; to triumph and gloat over someone (Phebe gloats over poor Silvius).

(ii) **the ordinary**: the common run, the usual and unremarkable sort (here, the ordinary products of nature's workshop, so Phebe is no better than ordinary women).

(iii) **inky brows**: eyebrows as black as ink, that is, very dark eyebrows.

(iv) **properer**: more handsome, finer-looking and of better worth ("proper" meant handsome or fine in Shakespeare's time).

**e.** Pick out two figures of speech used in the passage and show how effectively they have been used. *(2/2 = 4 marks)*

Any two, named, quoted and explained:

- **Simile**: "Like foggy south, puffing with wind and rain" compares Silvius's sighs and tears to a damp south wind; it shows how useless and tiresome his pleading is, and makes Rosalind's scorn clear.
- **Rhetorical questions**: "Why, what means this? Why do you look on me?" are not meant to be answered; they attack Phebe's pride and make her look foolish.
- **Hyperbole**: "a thousand times a properer man" exaggerates Silvius's worth to shame Phebe into valuing him.
- **Sarcasm / irony**: "Od's my little life ... I think she means to tangle my eyes too!" mocks Phebe's claim to power over men's eyes.

(Any other correctly named and explained device is accepted.)

**f.** Give an account of the rest of the scene from which this extract is taken. *(2/2/2 = 6 marks)*

The extract comes from the scene in the forest where Rosalind (as Ganymede) rebukes Phebe (Act 3, Scene 5). In the rest of the scene:

1. Rosalind finishes her rebuke by advising Phebe to accept Silvius's love while she can, because she is unlikely to get a better offer, and she leaves with Celia and Corin.
2. **Phebe, who has fallen in love with the "young man" Ganymede** at first sight, is struck by what she has heard; she admits that the old saying about love at first sight is true.
3. She questions Silvius about Ganymede and agrees to keep Silvius as a friend, so that he can carry a letter for her. She decides to write Ganymede a sharp letter, and Silvius goes with her.

**d.** Pick and name any two figures of speech from the extract and show their effectiveness. *(3+3 = 6 marks)*

Any two, each named (1 mark), quoted (1 mark) and explained (1 mark):

- **Comparison with exaggeration (hyperbole)**: "No Nightingale did ever chant / More welcome notes to weary bands / Of travellers" - the girl's song is said to be sweeter than the nightingale's, which shows how beautiful it is to the poet.
- **Apostrophe / imperative**: "Behold her ... Stop here, or gently pass!" - the poet speaks directly to the reader and draws him into the scene.
- **Metaphor / exaggeration**: "the vale profound / Is overflowing with the sound" - the valley is pictured as a bowl so full of song that it overflows.
- **Imagery**: "Breaking the silence of the seas" - the song is like a voice heard across a still, silent sea.
- **Repetition / alliteration**: "solitary" and "singing", "sings a melancholy strain".

**e.** Give an account of the rest of the poem. *(2+2+2+1 = 7 marks)*

The extract gives the first two stanzas. In the rest of the poem (stanzas 3 and 4):

1. The poet wonders what the girl is singing about, since he cannot understand her language; he asks if someone can tell him.
2. He suggests that it may be a sad song about **old, unhappy, far-off things and battles long ago**, or something more humble and familiar, some natural sorrow, loss or pain.
3. Whatever the theme, he sees her sing as if her song would never end, bending over her sickle as she works.
4. He listens quietly and then climbs up the hill; **the music stays in his heart long after he can no longer hear it**.

**Part 1: Four difficulties (16 marks, 4 marks each).** For each: name it, say who suffers it, and describe it with an event.

1. **No adults and no rules at first**: the boys are alone on the island, and they must decide how to be governed; quarrels grow over who should lead.

4. **Division and violence between Ralph's group and Jack's hunters**: Jack leaves and takes most of the boys with him, and the savagery ends in the deaths of Simon and Piggy.

**Part 2: How the survivors work to overcome each (9 marks: 2/2/2/2 + 1).** (1) They call assemblies and elect a chief (Ralph), using the **conch** to give order; (2) they build a **signal fire** on the mountain top and take turns to keep it burning; (3) Ralph and the others try to **calm the fears with reason and discussion**; (4) Ralph and Piggy try to keep to the rules and to call assemblies and appeal to the boys' sense of order; one more mark for a clear comment on how they only partly succeed.

**SECTION A: DRAMA. WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: AS YOU LIKE IT.**

Read the following extract and answer the questions below it.

**Speaker A:**

Speak you so gently? Pardon me, I pray you.
I thought that all things had been savage here,
And therefore, put I on the countenance
Of stern commandment. But whate'er you are
That in this desert inaccessible, *(5)*
Under the shade of melancholy boughs,
Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time;
If ever you have looked on better days,
If ever been where bells have knolled to church,
If ever sat at any good man's feast, *(10)*
If ever from your eyelids wiped a tear,
And know what 't is to pity and be pitied,
Let gentleness my strong enforcement be;
In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword.

**Speaker B:**

True is it that we have seen better days, *(15)*
And have with holy bell been knolled to church,
And sat at good men's feasts, and wiped our eyes
Of drops that sacred pity hath engendered;
And therefore, sit you down in gentleness,
And take upon command what help we have *(20)*
That to your wanting may be ministered.

**a.** Identify speakers A and B. *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

**b.** Where are they? *(1 mark)*

**c.** Give the meaning of the following words and expressions as used in the extract.

(i) savage *(Line 2)* *(2 marks)*

(ii) commandment *(Line 4)* *(2 marks)*

(iii) sacred pity *(Line 18)* *(2 marks)*

(iv) wanting *(Line 21)* *(2 marks)*

**d.** State and explain two character traits of Speaker A as revealed in the passage. *(2/2 = 4 marks)*

**e.** Pick and name any two literary devices used in the extract. *(2/2 = 4 marks)*

**f.** Give a brief account of what happens at the beginning of the scene from which this extract has been taken. *(2/2/2 = 6 marks)*

**a.** Identify speakers A and B. *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

**Speaker A is Orlando** and **Speaker B is Duke Senior** (the banished Duke, living in the Forest of Arden). Orlando is the one who has burst in with a drawn sword ("I ... hide my sword"); the Duke is the one who answers him kindly and invites him to sit down.

**b.** Where are they? *(1 mark)*

They are in the **Forest of Arden**, at the Duke's camp in the forest, where the banished Duke and his lords are about to eat a meal (the extract itself says "this desert inaccessible" and "sit you down"). (Act 2, Scene 7.)

**c.** Give the meaning of the following words and expressions as used in the extract.

(i) savage *(Line 2)* *(2 marks)*

(ii) commandment *(Line 4)* *(2 marks)*

(iii) sacred pity *(Line 18)* *(2 marks)*

(iv) wanting *(Line 21)* *(2 marks)*

(i) **savage**: wild, uncivilised, fierce and without kindness (Orlando thought the people in the forest would be rough and cruel).

(ii) **commandment**: command, authority; "the countenance of stern commandment" means a stern, commanding look.

(iii) **sacred pity**: holy, deep compassion for others in distress.

(iv) **wanting**: need, lack; what you are short of (here, the food Orlando lacks).

**d.** State and explain two character traits of Speaker A as revealed in the passage. *(2/2 = 4 marks)*

Two traits, each supported from the extract:

1. **Polite and humble.** When he finds the Duke speaks "gently", Orlando at once says "Pardon me, I pray you" and admits he was wrong to think everyone in the forest was "savage". He blushes and puts away his sword ("I blush, and hide my sword").
2. **Desperate and bold, but at heart gentle and compassionate.** He first came in with a stern look and a drawn sword because of his need, yet he appeals to the Duke's pity ("If ever ... wiped a tear, / And know what 't is to pity and be pitied"). He asks for gentleness, not force.

(Other acceptable traits, if explained from the text: respectful, quick to change his mind, a man of good upbringing.)

**e.** Pick and name any two literary devices used in the extract. *(2/2 = 4 marks)*

Any two, named and illustrated:

- **Repetition / anaphora**: "If ever ... If ever ... If ever ..." (lines 8 to 11) repeats the same opening to build up an appeal to the Duke's sympathy.
- **Personification**: "the creeping hours of time" (line 7) gives time the movement of a living creature.
- **Metaphor**: "this desert inaccessible" describes the forest as a desert.
- **Imagery**: "the shade of melancholy boughs" creates a sad, lonely picture of the forest.

**f.** Give a brief account of what happens at the beginning of the scene from which this extract has been taken. *(2/2/2 = 6 marks)*

The extract is from Act 2, Scene 7. At the beginning of the scene, **Duke Senior and his lords are in the forest getting ready to eat**. The Duke notices that **Jaques** is missing. Jaques then comes in, delighted, having met **a fool** in the forest (Touchstone) who spoke wise things, and he says he wants to wear the fool's coloured coat so that he can speak freely and criticise the world. The Duke warns him about his sharp tongue. **It is then that Orlando bursts in with his sword drawn**, demanding food for himself and his old servant Adam, who is faint with hunger, and this is where the extract begins.

**Speaker A:**

I prithee, shepherd, if that love or gold
Can in this desert place buy entertainment,
Bring us where we may rest ourselves and feed.
Here's a young maid with travel much oppressed,
And faints for succour. *(5)*

**Speaker B:**

Fair sir, I pity her,
And wish, for her sake more than for mine own,
My fortunes were more able to relieve her;
But I am shepherd to another man,
And do not shear the fleeces that I graze.
My master is of churlish disposition, *(10)*
And little recks to find the way to heaven
By doing deeds of hospitality.
Besides, his cote, his flocks, and bounds of feed
Are now on sale, and at our sheepcote now,
By reason of his absence, there is nothing *(15)*
That you will feed on; but what is, come see,
And in my voice most welcome shall you be.

**a.** (i) Identify Speakers A and B. *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

(ii) Where is the conversation taking place? Who else is present? *(1/1 = 2 marks)*

**b.** What is the condition of the "young maid" (line 4) and what relationship does the young maid have with Speaker A? *(2/2 = 4 marks)*
